tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
##### EVALUATION.md (db-train-model)
# Evaluation: trip-delay forecasts against the baselines

How the fine-tuned time-series language model (TSLM) was scored, what it was scored against, and
what the numbers say. Every number below is produced by the scripts named in the last section; the
run-by-run detail is in `DESIGN.md` section 16 and the command of every job in `trip/RUNS.md`.
Times are Zurich. Rows marked *pending* are filled in as the last jobs finish.

## 1. The task being scored

One example is one train at one prediction moment with one target stop: given everything known at
that moment, forecast the arrival delay at the target stop in whole minutes, and the chance that
the train is cancelled. The forecast is a full distribution over minutes (read off the model's
next-token probabilities, one token per minute), from which the median, a 10 to 90% range and
P(late by 6 minutes or more) follow. A connection's chance of being made is derived from two such
distributions (`trip/connection.py`).

## 2. Data and splits

- **Source:** public DB timetable and change feeds, November 2025 to August 2026, processed into
  298,430 examples (`trip/build.py`). Every input is computed from records timestamped before the
  prediction moment; the target comes from the final arrival record. `test_build.py` checks the
  cutoffs.
- **Time split, no shuffling:** train before 1 May 2026 (174,070), validation May (30,622), test
  June to August (93,738). Hyper-parameters, blend weights and calibration were chosen on
  validation only.
- **Shared 5,000-example test subset:** every 2,000- and 5,000-step run is scored on the same
  5,000 test examples (`--test-limit 5000`, fixed seed), so runs compare like for like. Long runs
  are scored on all 93,738.
- **September forward set:** after the training data was frozen, the September 2026 feeds were
  scraped (last change feed 12 September, 19:50 local) and built with the same code
  (`forward.parquet`, 21,982 test examples from 1 September on; 10,000 scored). No model or blend
  weight was fitted on it. It is the honest "future" test.
- **Dataset variants:** `examples_v2`/`v3` add the arrival delays of the previous trains of the
  same type towards the same destination at the stop (up to five, within six hours, arrived before
  the prediction moment). Baselines are retrained on the same columns whenever a model uses them,
  so the comparison never rests on the TSLM seeing more data.

## 3. Metrics

All in minutes, lower is better, computed by `trip/metrics.py` on trips that ran (cancelled trips
count only in the cancellation metrics).

| Metric | What it measures |
|---|---|
| Median error (MAE of the median) | Distance between the distribution's median and the true delay |
| CRPS | Quality of the whole distribution: 19 quantiles (5% to 95%), pinball loss averaged; the standard proper score for probabilistic forecasts (Gneiting and Raftery 2007) |
| Coverage and width of the 10 to 90% range | Whether the range contains the truth about 80% of the time, and how wide it is |
| Brier score, late | Calibration of P(delay ≥ 6 min) |
| Log loss, cancelled | Calibration of P(cancelled) |

Every score is also broken down by train class (S-Bahn, regional, long-distance) and by lead time
(up to 15, 15 to 30, 30 to 60, 60 to 120, more than 120 minutes before the planned arrival).

**Significance.** Two models are compared with a paired bootstrap (`trip/bootstrap.py`): the
shared examples are resampled 2,000 times, both models are scored on each resample, and the 95%
interval of the difference is reported. A difference whose interval excludes zero is called real;
one that straddles zero is reported as "no clear difference". Two identical trainings of the same
recipe differ by 0.006 CRPS on the 5,000 examples, which is the noise floor for single runs.

## 4. Baselines

| Baseline | Inputs |
|---|---|
| Persistence | The current delay carries to the target stop; cancellation from the route's history |
| Route history | The route's 30-day delay distribution at the stop |
| XGBoost | Gradient-boosted trees (quantile, late and cancellation models) on the same engineered features the TSLM reads: current delay and trend, route history at three scales, station and network lateness over 3, 24 and 72 hours, lead time, stops ahead, train class and type, hour and weekday, and where present the previous trains on the route |

XGBoost is the one to beat: same information, a strong tabular learner, no language model.

## 5. Results

### 5.1 Shared 5,000 test examples (June to August)

Median error / CRPS. "Partner" names the run each experiment is compared with.

| Model | Median error | CRPS | vs XGBoost (CRPS, 95% interval) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Persistence | 3.990 | 3.316 | +0.345 |
| Route history | 5.873 | 4.999 | |
| XGBoost | 3.698 | 2.971 | |
| TSLM, original recipe (soft targets, encoder), 2k steps | 3.711 | 2.994 | +0.023 |
| TSLM, plain loss, encoder, 2k | 3.702 | 2.954 | -0.018 (-0.073 to +0.030) |
| TSLM, plain loss, encoder, 5k | 3.678 | 2.923 | -0.048 |
| TSLM, text input, plain loss, 2k | 3.635 | 2.907 | -0.064 (-0.137 to -0.005) real |
| TSLM, text input, plain + CRPS loss, 2k | 3.621 | 2.903 | |
| TSLM, text input, plain loss, 5k | 3.614 | 2.883 | |
| TSLM, encoder only, plain + CRPS loss, 12k | 3.602 | 2.889 | -0.082 (-0.137 to -0.041) real; within 15 min -0.112, beyond 30 min -0.072, both real |
| XGBoost retrained with previous trains (v2 data) | 3.654 | 2.937 | |
| TSLM, text, v2 data, 2k | 3.616 | 2.889 | -0.048 vs XGBoost-v2 (-0.121 to +0.010) |
| TSLM, text + encoder, v2 data, 2k | 3.603 | 2.877 | -0.060 vs XGBoost-v2 (-0.130 to -0.005) real |
| Lead-time blend, text + plain, 2k | 3.618 | 2.901 | -0.070 (-0.127 to -0.030) real |
| Lead-time blend, text + encoder, v2 data | | | -0.049 vs XGBoost-v2 (-0.100 to -0.015) real |
| TSLM, text with XGBoost's forecast in the prompt (stacked, v4 data), 2k | 3.573 | 2.860 | -0.075 vs XGBoost-v3 (-0.116 to -0.044) real; within 15 min -0.086, beyond 30 min -0.085, both real |

### 5.2 All 93,738 test examples

| Model | Median error | CRPS | vs XGBoost (CRPS) |
|---|---|---|---|
| XGBoost | 3.462 | 2.759 | |
| XGBoost, v2 data | 3.413 | 2.723 | |
| TSLM, plain loss, encoder, 2k | 3.477 | 2.774 | +0.015 |
| Lead-time blend of that with XGBoost | 3.427 | 2.731 | -0.028 (-0.039 to -0.019) real; median error -0.035 |
| TSLM, original recipe, 12k (30,000 of the test) | 3.434 | 2.754 | XGBoost on the same 30,000: 3.469 / 2.765; median error real |
| Final: text + encoder, plain loss, 12k | 3.397 | 2.699 | -0.060 (-0.073 to -0.048) real; median error -0.066 real; within 15 min -0.091 real; beyond 30 min -0.046 real; lead-time blend -0.067 |

## 6. What the ablations established

Each experiment changes one ingredient against a named partner on the shared 5,000 examples;
details and intervals in `DESIGN.md` section 16.

- **Exact-minute loss beats soft targets** (-0.041 CRPS, -0.069 to -0.011). Soft targets blur the
  distribution; the cross-entropy on the exact minute lets the model keep it sharp, and adding a
  CRPS term (`plain_crps`) rewards near misses through a proper score instead. It is the loss of
  the final runs.
- **At 2,000 steps, writing the series into the prompt beats the time-series encoder** (-0.057,
  -0.090 to -0.026), and the encoder adds nothing on top of the text on the original data.
  Eleven encoder-side changes (raw scale, series-reading curriculum, 720-point series, a
  pretrained or random start, a five-times faster encoder, training the encoder alone or first)
  all land within noise of the encoder baseline or below it. With the richer v2 data the
  text-plus-encoder model is the best 2,000-step run, 0.013 ahead of text alone (inside the noise).
- **Given enough steps, the encoder path catches up.** Encoder only for 12,000 steps reaches the
  best validation score of all runs and beats XGBoost at every lead time on the shared test
  (-0.082 overall, -0.072 beyond 30 minutes), level with the text model at 5,000 steps (+0.006,
  -0.044 to +0.062), and beats XGBoost alone on the September set as well (-0.033). The series
  channel carries the same information as the text and needs about twice the training to extract
  it.
- **More training keeps helping** (2k to 5k: -0.024 CRPS for text); the long runs are the finals.
- **The statistical forecast as an input makes the TSLM win everywhere.** With XGBoost's own
  median, range and probabilities written into the prompt as one sentence (out-of-fold on the
  training split), the model corrects the tabular forecast: -0.075 CRPS on the shared test at
  every lead time, and -0.039 alone on September, out of time. The lead-time blend then has
  nothing to add (fitted weight 1.0).
- **Richer data helps both sides equally:** the previous trains on the route improve XGBoost by
  0.036 and the TSLM by 0.018 on the full test, and the TSLM keeps its edge against the retrained
  baseline.
- **Multi-scale history summaries** (90-day and 7-day medians, same-hour lateness) improve
  validation but not test.
- **Calibration is already good:** temperature and Platt re-scaling chosen on validation leave the
  minute distribution as it is; only P(cancelled) benefits from mostly following XGBoost in the
  blend.

## 7. Limits, stated plainly

- Without the statistical forecast in the prompt, a single 2,000-step TSLM does not beat XGBoost
  across the board; the wins are within 15 minutes of arrival and through the lead-time blend.
  With it, the 2,000-step model wins at every lead time and out of time; the 12,000-step finals
  say by how much.
- The encoder, the part of OpenTSLM built for time series, learns more slowly than the text
  channel on this data and adds nothing on top of it at 2,000 steps; at 12,000 steps alone it
  matches the text and beats the tabular baseline.
- Differences of 0.01 to 0.03 CRPS between single runs on 5,000 examples are inside the noise;
  only the full-test and bootstrap-backed claims above should be quoted.
- The September set is scraped from the live feeds and covers 12 days; its XGBoost partner was
  trained on the same May data as the TSLM, so neither side saw the summer.

## 8. Reproducing the numbers

```bash
# examples, baselines, shared metrics
python trip/build.py --raw data/raw --out data/trip/examples.parquet
python trip/baselines.py --examples data/trip/examples.parquet --out out/trip/baselines
# one TSLM run (an H100 job runs exactly this; see trip/RUNS.md for every job's arguments)
python trip/train.py --out out/trip/run --max-steps 2000 --loss-mode plain_crps --prompt-mode text --test-limit 5000
# blend weights on validation, scored on test; then the paired bootstrap
python trip/combine.py --run out/trip/run --baselines out/trip/baselines
python trip/bootstrap.py --a tslm=out/trip/run/tslm_test.npz --b xgb=out/trip/baselines/xgboost_test.npz
python trip/bootstrap.py --a blend=out/trip/run/blend_lead_test.npz --b xgb=out/trip/baselines/xgboost_test.npz --lead-max 15
# September forward test: XGBoost scored on the forward set, a checkpoint scored on it, May weights applied blind
python trip/baselines.py --examples data/trip/examples.parquet --out out/trip/baselines_forward --extra-examples data/trip/forward.parquet
python trip/train.py --eval-only --resume out/trip/run/checkpoint.pt --loss-mode plain_crps --prompt-mode text \
    --examples data/trip/forward.parquet --test-limit 10000 --generate 0 --out out/trip/forward_run
python trip/apply_blend.py --weights out/trip/run/combine.json --tslm out/trip/forward_run/tslm_test.npz \
    --xgb out/trip/baselines_forward/xgboost_forward.npz --examples data/trip/forward.parquet \
    --out out/trip/forward_run/blend_lead_test.npz
```

##### EVALUATION.md (db-train-model)
# Evaluation: trip-delay forecasts against the baselines

How the fine-tuned time-series language model (TSLM) was scored, what it was scored against, and
what the numbers say. Every number below is produced by the scripts named in the last section; the
run-by-run detail is in `DESIGN.md` section 16 and the command of every job in `trip/RUNS.md`.
Times are Zurich. Rows marked *pending* are filled in as the last jobs finish.

## 1. The task being scored

One example is one train at one prediction moment with one target stop: given everything known at
that moment, forecast the arrival delay at the target stop in whole minutes, and the chance that
the train is cancelled. The forecast is a full distribution over minutes (read off the model's
next-token probabilities, one token per minute), from which the median, a 10 to 90% range and
P(late by 6 minutes or more) follow. A connection's chance of being made is derived from two such
distributions (`trip/connection.py`).

## 2. Data and splits

- **Source:** public DB timetable and change feeds, November 2025 to August 2026, processed into
  298,430 examples (`trip/build.py`). Every input is computed from records timestamped before the
  prediction moment; the target comes from the final arrival record. `test_build.py` checks the
  cutoffs.
- **Time split, no shuffling:** train before 1 May 2026 (174,070), validation May (30,622), test
  June to August (93,738). Hyper-parameters, blend weights and calibration were chosen on
  validation only.
- **Shared 5,000-example test subset:** every 2,000- and 5,000-step run is scored on the same
  5,000 test examples (`--test-limit 5000`, fixed seed), so runs compare like for like. Long runs
  are scored on all 93,738.
- **September forward set:** after the training data was frozen, the September 2026 feeds were
  scraped (last change feed 12 September, 19:50 local) and built with the same code
  (`forward.parquet`, 21,982 test examples from 1 September on; 10,000 scored). No model or blend
  weight was fitted on it. It is the honest "future" test.
- **Dataset variants:** `examples_v2`/`v3` add the arrival delays of the previous trains of the
  same type towards the same destination at the stop (up to five, within six hours, arrived before
  the prediction moment). Baselines are retrained on the same columns whenever a model uses them,
  so the comparison never rests on the TSLM seeing more data.

## 3. Metrics

All in minutes, lower is better, computed by `trip/metrics.py` on trips that ran (cancelled trips
count only in the cancellation metrics).

| Metric | What it measures |
|---|---|
| Median error (MAE of the median) | Distance between the distribution's median and the true delay |
| CRPS | Quality of the whole distribution: 19 quantiles (5% to 95%), pinball loss averaged; the standard proper score for probabilistic forecasts (Gneiting and Raftery 2007) |
| Coverage and width of the 10 to 90% range | Whether the range contains the truth about 80% of the time, and how wide it is |
| Brier score, late | Calibration of P(delay ≥ 6 min) |
| Log loss, cancelled | Calibration of P(cancelled) |

Every score is also broken down by train class (S-Bahn, regional, long-distance) and by lead time
(up to 15, 15 to 30, 30 to 60, 60 to 120, more than 120 minutes before the planned arrival).

**Significance.** Two models are compared with a paired bootstrap (`trip/bootstrap.py`): the
shared examples are resampled 2,000 times, both models are scored on each resample, and the 95%
interval of the difference is reported. A difference whose interval excludes zero is called real;
one that straddles zero is reported as "no clear difference". Two identical trainings of the same
recipe differ by 0.006 CRPS on the 5,000 examples, which is the noise floor for single runs.

## 4. Baselines

| Baseline | Inputs |
|---|---|
| Persistence | The current delay carries to the target stop; cancellation from the route's history |
| Route history | The route's 30-day delay distribution at the stop |
| XGBoost | Gradient-boosted trees (quantile, late and cancellation models) on the same engineered features the TSLM reads: current delay and trend, route history at three scales, station and network lateness over 3, 24 and 72 hours, lead time, stops ahead, train class and type, hour and weekday, and where present the previous trains on the route |

XGBoost is the one to beat: same information, a strong tabular learner, no language model.

only the stacked model beats XGBoost alone out of time, so stacking is what carries it.

### 5.5 The same results in minutes

CRPS scores the whole distribution; these figures read the predicted median only
(`trip/plain_metrics.py`, cancelled trains left out). "Within 1 minute" means the forecast was
off by at most one minute. The range column should be near 80%.

Full test, 88,479 trains:

| Model | Average miss | Within 1 min | Within 2 min | Within 5 min | Bias | Truth inside 10 to 90% range |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Persistence (delay carried forward) | 3.75 min | 62% | 72% | 86% | -2.17 | 84% |
| XGBoost, combined features | 3.41 min | 57% | 71% | 85% | -1.76 | 82% |
| XGBoost, plus same-train and corridor series | 3.28 min | 59% | 72% | 86% | -1.70 | 82% |
| TSLM, text final, 12k | 3.32 min | 65% | 75% | 87% | -1.80 | 90% |
| TSLM, stacked text final, 12k | 3.33 min | 65% | 74% | 86% | -1.57 | 89% |

Within 15 minutes of the planned arrival (36,556 trains): persistence 84% within one minute,
XGBoost 78% and 81%, both TSLM finals 86%.

The 5,000 shared test trains, by class (share within one minute / average miss):

| Model | S-Bahn | Regional | Long-distance |
|---|---|---|---|
| XGBoost, plus new series | 77% / 0.93 min | 72% / 1.58 min | 29% / 7.73 min |
| TSLM, text on the new series, 2k | 85% / 0.90 min | 79% / 1.56 min | 34% / 7.61 min |

- **The language model is right to the minute more often:** 65% against 57 to 59% over the full
  test, in every class and every lead-time bucket.
- **The average miss hides a heavy tail.** All models predict slightly too early on average and the
  spread of the error is 10 to 13 minutes for every one of them, driven by a few very long delays
  none of them foresees; the share within 1, 2 and 5 minutes is the honest summary.
- **Without fine-tuning** the same checkpoint on the same prompts misses by 3.55 minutes on average
  (it mostly repeats the XGBoost forecast in the prompt) but its distribution is far off: CRPS
  +0.347 against the trained model, and none of its generated answers is in the answer format.
- **Every run in the same figures:** `trip/MINUTES.md` (34 runs and baselines on the same 4,729
  test trains).
- **The TSLM's range is a little too wide** (88 to 90% of true delays inside the 10 to 90% range,
  against 82% for XGBoost): cautious rather than overconfident.

## 6. What the ablations established

Each experiment changes one ingredient against a named partner on the shared 5,000 examples;
details and intervals in `DESIGN.md` section 16.

- **Exact-minute loss beats soft targets** (-0.041 CRPS, -0.069 to -0.011). Soft targets blur the
  distribution; the cross-entropy on the exact minute lets the model keep it sharp, and adding a
  CRPS term (`plain_crps`) rewards near misses through a proper score instead. It is the loss of
  the final runs.
- **At 2,000 steps, writing the series into the prompt beats the time-series encoder** (-0.057,
  -0.090 to -0.026), and the encoder adds nothing on top of the text on the original data.
  Eleven encoder-side changes (raw scale, series-reading curriculum, 720-point series, a
  pretrained or random start, a five-times faster encoder, training the encoder alone or first)
  all land within noise of the encoder baseline or below it. With the richer v2 data the
  text-plus-encoder model is the best 2,000-step run, 0.013 ahead of text alone (inside the noise).
- **Given enough steps, the encoder path catches up.** Encoder only for 12,000 steps reaches the
  best validation score of all runs and beats XGBoost at every lead time on the shared test
  (-0.082 overall, -0.072 beyond 30 minutes), level with the text model at 5,000 steps (+0.006,
  -0.044 to +0.062), and beats XGBoost alone on the September set as well (-0.033). The series
  channel carries the same information as the text and needs about twice the training to extract
  it.
- **More training keeps helping** (2k to 5k: -0.024 CRPS for text); the long runs are the finals.
- **The statistical forecast as an input makes the TSLM win everywhere.** With XGBoost's own
  median, range and probabilities written into the prompt as one sentence (out-of-fold on the
  training split), the model corrects the tabular forecast: -0.075 CRPS on the shared test at
  every lead time, and -0.039 alone on September, out of time. The lead-time blend then has
  nothing to add (fitted weight 1.0).
- **Richer data helps both sides equally:** the previous trains on the route improve XGBoost by
  0.036 and the TSLM by 0.018 on the full test, and the TSLM keeps its edge against the retrained
  baseline.
- **Multi-scale history summaries** (90-day and 7-day medians, same-hour lateness) improve
  validation but not test.
- **Calibration is already good:** temperature and Platt re-scaling chosen on validation leave the
  minute distribution as it is; only P(cancelled) benefits from mostly following XGBoost in the
  blend.

## 7. Limits, stated plainly

- Without the statistical forecast in the prompt, a single 2,000-step TSLM does not beat XGBoost
  across the board; the wins are within 15 minutes of arrival and through the lead-time blend.
  With it, the 2,000-step model wins at every lead time and out of time; the 12,000-step finals
  say by how much.
- The encoder, the part of OpenTSLM built for time series, learns more slowly than the text
  channel on this data and adds nothing on top of it at 2,000 steps; at 12,000 steps alone it
  matches the text and beats the tabular baseline.
- Differences of 0.01 to 0.03 CRPS between single runs on 5,000 examples are inside the noise;
  only the full-test and bootstrap-backed claims above should be quoted.
- The September set is scraped from the live feeds and covers 12 days; its XGBoost partner was
  trained on the same May data as the TSLM, so neither side saw the summer.

## 8. Reproducing the numbers

```bash
# examples, baselines, shared metrics
python trip/build.py --raw data/raw --out data/trip/examples.parquet
python trip/baselines.py --examples data/trip/examples.parquet --out out/trip/baselines
# one TSLM run (an H100 job runs exactly this; see trip/RUNS.md for every job's arguments)
python trip/train.py --out out/trip/run --max-steps 2000 --loss-mode plain_crps --prompt-mode text --test-limit 5000
# blend weights on validation, scored on test; then the paired bootstrap
python trip/combine.py --run out/trip/run --baselines out/trip/baselines
python trip/bootstrap.py --a tslm=out/trip/run/tslm_test.npz --b xgb=out/trip/baselines/xgboost_test.npz
python trip/bootstrap.py --a blend=out/trip/run/blend_lead_test.npz --b xgb=out/trip/baselines/xgboost_test.npz --lead-max 15
# September forward test: XGBoost scored on the forward set, a checkpoint scored on it, May weights applied blind
python trip/baselines.py --examples data/trip/examples.parquet --out out/trip/baselines_forward --extra-examples data/trip/forward.parquet
python trip/train.py --eval-only --resume out/trip/run/checkpoint.pt --loss-mode plain_crps --prompt-mode text \
    --examples data/trip/forward.parquet --test-limit 10000 --generate 0 --out out/trip/forward_run
python trip/apply_blend.py --weights out/trip/run/combine.json --tslm out/trip/forward_run/tslm_test.npz \
    --xgb out/trip/baselines_forward/xgboost_forward.npz --examples data/trip/forward.parquet \
    --out out/trip/forward_run/blend_lead_test.npz
```

## Reading

- **Quarter (6 h × 60 d) wins every cell.** Lowest error on both held-out cells and the smallest seen→unseen gap (0.13 min); week (7 d hourly) memorises — 0.6 min worse on unseen trains than on seen ones.
- **Multiscale does not add.** The plan's additivity question (does long history help *on top of* the week?) gets a no at this budget: second-worst on every cell. Caveat: it carries 2.8× the encoder tokens of the others and saw the identical 16k samples, so a fixed step budget under-trains the largest input.
- **The TSLM ties the tabular baseline on unseen trains** (quarter/test: 1.820 vs 1.816, CRPS 1.370 vs 1.374) and trails it by ~0.08 min on seen trains at 2k steps — the regime the literature predicts (RIDE: XGBoost within 4% of the best deep model) and what the trip-delay work found before its 12k-step runs.
- **The blend is the best forecast on every cell**, and the TSLM's fitted share rises with profile quality: 0.15 (week) → 0.20 (season) → 0.30 (quarter).
- **Publish `test` (unseen trains and weeks) as the headline and the gap to `test_seen_entity` as the memorisation estimate.** `test_seen_time` is optimistic by construction and is reported, not headlined.
- Everything is ~30% under the naive train-median baseline; 10–90% coverage sits at 0.70–0.80 against a 0.80 target, so the distributions are slightly narrow.

Artifacts: `s3://error404-db-route/runs/route-2k/<profile>/{metrics.json, checkpoint.pt, scalar_<cell>.npz}`; local baselines/blend in `baselines_local.json` beside them.

##### TRAINING.md (multiscale)
# Training the db-route datasets

The recipe is `db_delay/trip` (Jonas): OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt on Llama-3.2-3B from the published
`OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-3b-m4-sp` encoder, LoRA on, a minute-distribution readout after `Answer:`.
`train_route.py` points it at our TimeF registry through `bridge.py`; the loss accepts our three
non-minute tasks as plain cross-entropy. One profile per GPU.

## Environment: why it is not the PyTorch image

`opentslm` needs Python ≥ 3.12; `pytorch/pytorch:*-runtime` images ship 3.11, so every job on
them dies at `pip install`. Use the bare CUDA image and build the venv in `--setup`, exactly as
`trip/nebius/run_ablations.sh` does — `nebius_setup_train.sh` is that step and
`requirements_train.txt` is Jonas's devbox freeze plus `timenet`, `timenet-connectors`, `pytz`,
`xgboost`. The requirements file is read from the bucket (`code/requirements_train.txt`), not
injected, because the backend would otherwise run it through the image's system pip.

## Submit (one job per profile; H100 NVLink = `gpu-h100-sxm`)

```bash
SC=…/scratchpad  # or anywhere; the two files are in this folder
for p in week quarter season multiscale; do
  npm --prefix app/backend run -s train -- submit --name route-2k-$p \
    --script $PWD/app/agents/src/features/db_route/train_route.py \
    --image nvidia/cuda:13.1.1-runtime-ubuntu24.04 \
    --setup "$(cat app/agents/src/features/db_route/nebius_setup_train.sh)" \
    --platform gpu-h100-sxm --preset 1gpu-16vcpu-200gb \
    --output storagebucket-e0016098467606655017642 --timeout 4h --disk-gib 100 \
    --env RUN_TAG=route-2k --env HF_HOME=/workspace/hf \
    -- --profiles $p --grad-checkpointing --steps 2000 --tag route-2k
done
```

A multi-GPU preset runs the same script under `torchrun`, with rank *i* → profile *i* of
`--profiles`; the 4×L40S preset would not provision tonight, the 1-GPU H100 preset did in under a
minute. Inputs: `code/db_route.tar.gz` and `registry/` in the bucket. Outputs:
`runs/<tag>/<profile>/{metrics.json, checkpoint.pt, scalar_<cell>.npz}`.

## What gets scored

Per split cell (`val`, `test_seen_entity`, `test`, `test_seen_time`): median error, CRPS,
10–90% coverage and width, Brier for late ≥ 5 min — for the TSLM's minute distribution, the
eight-week habit as persistence, and an XGBoost on the same scalar annotations and caption levels.
`test_seen_entity` (known trains, unseen weeks) is the deployment number; `test` (unseen trains
and weeks) is the generalisation diagnostic. Classification tasks report generated-answer accuracy
against the majority class on a subsample.

## Reading

- **Quarter (6 h × 60 d) wins every cell.** Lowest error on both held-out cells and the smallest seen→unseen gap (0.13 min); week (7 d hourly) memorises — 0.6 min worse on unseen trains than on seen ones.
- **Multiscale does not add.** The plan's additivity question (does long history help *on top of* the week?) gets a no at this budget: second-worst on every cell. Caveat: it carries 2.8× the encoder tokens of the others and saw the identical 16k samples, so a fixed step budget under-trains the largest input.
- **The TSLM ties the tabular baseline on unseen trains** (quarter/test: 1.820 vs 1.816, CRPS 1.370 vs 1.374) and trails it by ~0.08 min on seen trains at 2k steps — the regime the literature predicts (RIDE: XGBoost within 4% of the best deep model) and what the trip-delay work found before its 12k-step runs.
- **The blend is the best forecast on every cell**, and the TSLM's fitted share rises with profile quality: 0.15 (week) → 0.20 (season) → 0.30 (quarter).
- **Publish `test` (unseen trains and weeks) as the headline and the gap to `test_seen_entity` as the memorisation estimate.** `test_seen_time` is optimistic by construction and is reported, not headlined.
- Everything is ~30% under the naive train-median baseline; 10–90% coverage sits at 0.70–0.80 against a 0.80 target, so the distributions are slightly narrow.

Artifacts: `s3://error404-db-route/runs/route-2k/<profile>/{metrics.json, checkpoint.pt, scalar_<cell>.npz}`; local baselines/blend in `baselines_local.json` beside them.

##### TRAINING.md (multiscale)
# Training the db-route datasets

The recipe is `db_delay/trip` (Jonas): OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt on Llama-3.2-3B from the published
`OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-3b-m4-sp` encoder, LoRA on, a minute-distribution readout after `Answer:`.
`train_route.py` points it at our TimeF registry through `bridge.py`; the loss accepts our three
non-minute tasks as plain cross-entropy. One profile per GPU.

## Environment: why it is not the PyTorch image

`opentslm` needs Python ≥ 3.12; `pytorch/pytorch:*-runtime` images ship 3.11, so every job on
them dies at `pip install`. Use the bare CUDA image and build the venv in `--setup`, exactly as
`trip/nebius/run_ablations.sh` does — `nebius_setup_train.sh` is that step and
`requirements_train.txt` is Jonas's devbox freeze plus `timenet`, `timenet-connectors`, `pytz`,
`xgboost`. The requirements file is read from the bucket (`code/requirements_train.txt`), not
injected, because the backend would otherwise run it through the image's system pip.

## Submit (one job per profile; H100 NVLink = `gpu-h100-sxm`)

```bash
SC=…/scratchpad  # or anywhere; the two files are in this folder
for p in week quarter season multiscale; do
  npm --prefix app/backend run -s train -- submit --name route-2k-$p \
    --script $PWD/app/agents/src/features/db_route/train_route.py \
    --image nvidia/cuda:13.1.1-runtime-ubuntu24.04 \
    --setup "$(cat app/agents/src/features/db_route/nebius_setup_train.sh)" \
    --platform gpu-h100-sxm --preset 1gpu-16vcpu-200gb \
    --output storagebucket-e0016098467606655017642 --timeout 4h --disk-gib 100 \
    --env RUN_TAG=route-2k --env HF_HOME=/workspace/hf \
    -- --profiles $p --grad-checkpointing --steps 2000 --tag route-2k
done
```

A multi-GPU preset runs the same script under `torchrun`, with rank *i* → profile *i* of
`--profiles`; the 4×L40S preset would not provision tonight, the 1-GPU H100 preset did in under a
minute. Inputs: `code/db_route.tar.gz` and `registry/` in the bucket. Outputs:
`runs/<tag>/<profile>/{metrics.json, checkpoint.pt, scalar_<cell>.npz}`.

## What gets scored

Per split cell (`val`, `test_seen_entity`, `test`, `test_seen_time`): median error, CRPS,
10–90% coverage and width, Brier for late ≥ 5 min — for the TSLM's minute distribution, the
eight-week habit as persistence, and an XGBoost on the same scalar annotations and caption levels.
`test_seen_entity` (known trains, unseen weeks) is the deployment number; `test` (unseen trains
and weeks) is the generalisation diagnostic. Classification tasks report generated-answer accuracy
against the majority class on a subsample.

content.content:
- **Causes add nothing measurable.** The codes are archived after the fact, so only codes of
  stops already passed are usable, and those mostly restate the delay the run already shows.

### Fifth wave: series the text did not have (05:20)

A probe of what XGBoost still gets wrong pointed at two histories no input carried
(`examples_v7`, `forward_v7`; same example ids as v4):

- **Same train, last 28 days:** the delay this train number gained or recovered between the
  current stop and the target on each previous day, arrivals strictly before `t0`.
- **Corridor:** trains that left the current stop in the last 3 hours and already reached the
  target, their gains and arrival delays, last 8 by arrival.

Coverage 98% and 82% of examples. Both lists enter the prompt as series (encoder only in `split`
mode) and as scalars for XGBoost; the rationale gets one sentence with the medians.

| Model | 5,000 shared test | Full test | September |
|---|---|---|---|
| XGBoost, combined features (v3) | 3.650 / 2.935 | 3.414 / 2.720 | 2.786 / 2.207 |
| XGBoost with the new series (v7) | 3.507 / 2.824 | 3.278 / 2.616 | 2.645 / 2.100 |
| TSLM, stacked text, v7, 2k | 3.449 / 2.761 | | |
| TSLM, stacked split, v7, 2k: run and previous trains as text, the long history and both new series through the encoder only | 3.450 / 2.771 | | 2.543 / 2.023 (10,000) |
| TSLM, stacked text, v7, 12k (final) | | *running, about 09:00* | |

- **The best single improvement of the night, and it helps the baseline too:** -0.111 CRPS for
  XGBoost on the shared test (-0.149 to -0.077), real at every lead time. XGBoost-v7 alone now beats
  the best finished TSLM final (2.616 vs 2.644 on the full test), so the submission comparison is
  against XGBoost-v7.
- **The first time the embeddings carry what the text does not, and it pays (06:05).** In `split`
  mode the two new series reach the model only through the encoder. After 2,000 steps it beats
  XGBoost-v7 on the shared test: CRPS -0.052 (-0.095 to -0.020) and median error -0.058, real;
  within 15 minutes -0.086 and beyond 30 minutes -0.038, both real; against the stacked text
  model on v4 -0.089 (-0.130 to -0.050). Validation 2.605 / 2.102, the best of all runs.
- **Written out, the same series do slightly better (06:10).** Stacked text on v7 after 2,000
  steps: CRPS -0.063 (-0.108 to -0.030) against XGBoost-v7, real; within 15 minutes -0.093 and
  beyond 30 minutes -0.053, both real. Against the split model -0.010 (-0.019 to -0.003), real
  but small; the encoder route costs a hundredth of a CRPS point for a shorter prompt.
- **The split model holds out of time (06:30).** On 10,000 September examples it beats XGBoost-v7
  alone: CRPS -0.040 (-0.080 to -0.015), median error -0.056 (-0.103 to -0.027), within 15

content.text:
Both branches' results are in, from the committed evaluation docs and the Entire checkpoint transcripts. One important caveat first: the two branches score different tasks on different data, so the absolute numbers are not directly comparable. Both use the same recipe, OpenTSLM on Llama 3.2 3B with a minute-distribution readout, and both report median error and CRPS in minutes, lower is better.

## db-train-model (arrival delay at a target stop, Jonas's lane)

Task: forecast arrival delay at the target stop for one train at one moment. 298k examples, time split, test is June to August with 93,738 rows, plus a September forward set nobody fitted on. Baseline to beat is XGBoost on the same features.

| Model | Full test (median err / CRPS) | September forward |
|---|---|---|
| Persistence | 3.75 / 3.32 | 3.64 / 2.99 |
| XGBoost, original features | 3.46 / 2.76 | 3.24 / 2.59 |
| XGBoost v7 (strongest baseline) | 3.28 / 2.62 | 2.65 / 2.10 |
| TSLM text final, 12k steps | 3.32 / 2.64 | 2.67 / 2.11 |
| TSLM stacked text final, 12k | 3.33 / 2.65 | pending |
| TSLM v7 split, 2k steps | 3.45 / 2.77 on 5k subset | 2.54 / 2.02 |
| TSLM v7 stacked text, 12k | still running at last commit | |

In plain minutes: the language model is right to the minute 65% of the time against 57 to 59% for XGBoost, and its 10 to 90% range contains the truth 89% of the time against 82%.

**Conclusion recorded on the branch:** the best model is the v7 split TSLM, which feeds the same-train and corridor series through the encoder. It beats the strongest XGBoost on the September forward set by 0.077 CRPS with the bootstrap interval clear of zero. Three ingredients made the difference: exact-minute loss instead of soft targets, writing the XGBoost forecast into the prompt (stacking), and the two new v7 series. At 2k steps a plain TSLM loses to XGBoost beyond 30 minutes and only wins within 15 minutes. Fine-tuning is essential: zero-shot is worse by 0.35 CRPS. The 12k-step v7 finals had not finished when the branch was last pushed.

## feat/db-route-multiscale (departure delay, all-Germany route datasets)

Task: departure delay on four dataset profiles that differ in history window. Only 2k steps per profile, 600 scored rows per cell, so this is a bake-off, not a final. Baseline is scikit-learn gradient boosting on the same information.

| Profile | Unseen trains and weeks, TSLM | GBM | Blend |
|---|---|---|---|
| week (7 d hourly) | 2.51 / 1.91 | 2.36 / 1.87 | 2.37 / 1.86 |
| quarter (6 h x 60 d) | 1.82 / 1.37 | 1.82 / 1.37 | 1.79 / 1.35 |
| season (1 d x 120 d) | 1.98 / 1.50 | 1.90 / 1.48 | 1.89 / 1.46 |
| multiscale (all three) | 2.43 / 1.87 | 2.36 / 1.83 | 2.33 / 1.83 |

Classification accuracy (late or on time, plus cause family) sits at 0.62 to 0.78 against a majority class of 0.30 to 0.45.

**Conclusion recorded on the branch:** the quarter profile wins every cell and generalises best, with only a 0.13 minute gap between seen and unseen trains. The week profile memorises. Multiscale adds nothing on this budget, and its blend weight came out at zero. The TSLM ties gradient boosting on unseen trains and trails it slightly on seen trains. Everything is about 30% under the naive train-median baseline. The session ended with one open decision: a 12k-step quarter run, roughly three hours on one H100, was proposed but never launched.

## Side by side and how to improve

- **db-train-model is further along.** It has 12k-step finals, a real out-of-time test, a bootstrap-backed win over the strongest baseline, and 34 ablations. The multiscale branch is a 2k-step sweep where the TSLM only ties its baseline.
- **The same lesson appears on both branches:** at 2k steps the TSLM roughly ties trees. It only pulls ahead with long training and stacking. That is the direct path for the multiscale branch.

Improvement levers, in order of expected payoff:

1. **Train the quarter profile for 12k steps.** On db-train-model, going from 2k to 12k turned a tie into a 0.06 to 0.08 CRPS win. This is the one unlaunched action on the multiscale branch.
2. **Stack the tabular forecast into the prompt.** Writing the XGBoost median, range and late probability into the prompt was the first change that made the TSLM win at every lead time on db-train-model. The multiscale branch has not tried it.
3. **Finish and read the v7 12k finals on db-train-model.** The 2k v7 split already beats XGBoost-v7 out of time. The 12k run is the submission model, and its number is still unrecorded.
4. **Add series the text lacks.** The largest single gain of the night on db-train-model came from the same-train 28-day gains and the corridor series, which also improved XGBoost by 0.11 CRPS. Look for equivalent features on the route datasets.
5. **Give multiscale an equal budget per token.** It carried 2.8 times the encoder tokens for the same 16k samples, so it was under-trained. Rerun it at a matched epoch count before concluding long history adds nothing.
6. **Calibrate the range.** The trip model's 10 to 90% range is slightly too wide at 89% coverage, and the route model's is slightly narrow at 70 to 80%. A temperature fit on validation is cheap on both.
7. **Watch the tail.** Every model's error spread is 10 to 13 minutes, driven by a few very long delays nobody predicts. The within 1, 2 and 5 minute shares are the honest headline for the demo, not the average miss.

Both fact sheets are in. The short answer: the multiscale branch is not trained on better or cleaner data than db-train-model. Both draw from the same archive. It is trained on a smaller, aggregated, and easier task where gradient boosting already saturates, so there is nothing left for the language model to win.

## The two datasets side by side

| | db-train-model (trip) | feat/db-route-multiscale (route) |
|---|---|---|
| Raw source | Hugging Face `piebro/deutsche-bahn-data`, Nov 2025 to Aug 2026, all Germany | Same archive, same months, all Germany |
| Retrieval | Scripts only, DuckDB over the parquet files | Scripts only, DuckDB with HTTP range reads. No agent or LLM in the loop |

Sources: `app/agents/src/features/db_route/sources.py`, `labels.py`, `profiles.py`, and the trip `build.py` and `prompts.py` on db-train-model.

## Why the route data does not pull ahead

- **The premise is wrong. The data is the same.** Both branches read the identical Hugging Face parquet files with identical date ranges. The route branch adds holidays and station metadata, and both branches extract cause codes. Nothing in the route pipeline is retrieved by an agent.

- **The route target is a weekly average, and its level is already in the tabular features.** The label is the mean departure delay over seven days. The eight-week habit median and the mean and standard deviation of every series are handed to XGBoost as plain numbers. A weekly average is mostly its own recent level, so trees read the answer straight off those scalars. The TSLM has to reconstruct the same level from z-scored series plus a caption. There is no shape information left that would let it win.

- **There is no live signal to exploit.** On db-train-model the language model wins within 15 minutes of arrival, because the run's current delay dominates there. The route task has no equivalent. It forecasts a week ahead from history alone, which is exactly the regime where trees were better on db-train-model too.

- **The dataset is 40 times smaller by design.** The design session chose roughly 3,000 entities times 5 anchors after reading that OpenTSLM's best results came from small corpora. That may hold for classification, but for a minute readout db-train-model showed steady gains from 2k to 12k to 24k steps on 174k examples. The route model has seen about two epochs of 4,000 records.

- **The answer carries no rationale.** In the trained build the rationale body is empty. On db-train-model the rationale paragraph is what lets the text channel beat the encoder at 2k steps. The route model gets none of that scaffolding.

- **The extra sources do not carry signal at this budget.** Only 30% of stops have a cause code. Cause shares enter as series through the encoder, and db-train-model established that the encoder path needs about 12k steps to extract what text gives at 2k. On db-train-model, cause text added nothing measurable even with 174k examples.

- **The tie is not measurable anyway.** The headline cell has 462 rows. The trip work found a noise floor of 0.006 CRPS on 5,000 rows. Differences of 0.004 minutes on 462 rows mean nothing either way.

- **One label caveat.** The route label averages over cancelled stops as well, and its test_seen_time cell has context overlap with training labels, which the code itself documents. Neither is fatal, but both add noise.

## Conclusion

The route branch did not build better data. It built a different, smoother question with less data and no live state, then trained it too little to let the encoder matter. Gradient boosting saturates on that question, so a tie is the expected outcome, and the Belgian RIDE benchmark cited in the design session predicts exactly this.

To make the route pipeline beat trees, four changes matter, in order:

1. Change the target from a weekly mean to a per-event departure delay at a given moment, with the run's live delay in the input. That is the trip formulation, and it is where the language model has its edge.
2. Grow the entity count by an order of magnitude and train 12k steps. Both branches agree that the encoder needs that budget.
3. Fill the rationale from the inputs, as the trip prompts do, so the text channel carries the reasoning.
4. Stack the XGBoost forecast into the prompt. On db-train-model that was the single change that made the TSLM win at every lead time.

If the goal is a demo that beats the baseline on Saturday, db-train-model already does it. The route pipeline's real assets are its all-Germany cause extraction, holiday features and disruption notices, and those can be joined onto the trip examples rather than trained on their own.

content.text:
The brief changes the framing but not the answer. The jury scores four things: a useful problem with sourced data, a TimeNet connector, a trained TSLM evaluated against a baseline on leakage-safe splits, and a demo. Here is how the two branches score on each.

| Brief criterion | db-train-model | feat/db-route-multiscale |
|---|---|---|
| Useful problem, target user | Strong. "How late will my train be, will I make my connection." Per-train, per-stop, actionable | Weaker. A weekly average delay per line and station. Useful for planners, not a traveller |
| Data sourcing | Scripted from one public archive | Same archive plus cause codes, holidays, disruption notices. No agentic sourcing on either branch |
| TimeNet connector | One connector, one dataset, TimeF export verified | Four registered connectors, a reusable pipeline, dataset manifests. The stronger connector story |
| Train and evaluate | Strong. 12k-step finals, 93,738 test rows, September out-of-time set, bootstrap intervals, beats the strongest XGBoost | Weak. 2k steps, 462 rows per cell, ties the baseline, though the seen/unseen 2x2 split design is good |
| Demonstration | Working. Model server behind the app's contract, real Göttingen connection example | Nothing serving. A generation script prints held-out prompts |

**Use db-train-model as the submission.** It wins on the three criteria the brief weights most: the problem, the evaluation, and the demo. It also satisfies the submission checklist today: checkpoint, training config in RUNS.md, dataset documentation in DESIGN.md, and a baseline evaluation in EVALUATION.md.

**Fold the multiscale branch into the story rather than the model.** The brief says reusable connectors and well-chosen data are especially valued. That is exactly what the route branch has and the trip branch lacks. Present its four connectors, its all-Germany cause extraction, and its leakage-aware split design as your data preparation work. Report the bake-off honestly as a learning: a weekly-average target saturates on trees, which is why you moved to per-train forecasting.

**One gap the brief exposes on both branches.** It encourages an agentic data-sourcing pipeline that searches, assesses and validates datasets. Neither branch has one. Both hard-code one Hugging Face archive. The design transcript shows an agent-driven dataset probe was planned but the shipped pipelines are plain scripts. If there is time before the pitch, that is the cheapest criterion left to claim, and the honest alternative is to state plainly that sourcing was manual.

**Limitations to state in the pitch,** since the brief asks for them: a single 2k-step TSLM does not beat XGBoost beyond 30 minutes ahead, the win comes from stacking and the v7 series, every model misses the rare very long delays, and the September set covers only twelve days.

No. The two branches predict different things.

| | db-train-model | feat/db-route-multiscale |
|---|---|---|
| Question | How late will this specific train arrive at this specific stop? | How late will this line usually depart from this station over the coming week? |
| Unit | One train run on one day, one target stop, one moment in time | One line and station pair, one travel date |
| Target | Arrival delay in whole minutes, or cancelled | Average departure delay over the next 7 days, to a tenth of a minute |
| Horizon | Minutes to a few hours ahead | One week ahead |
| Uses the train's live delay | Yes | No, history only |
| Output | A full minute distribution, plus P(late) and P(cancelled) | A single number, plus late or on time, plus the dominant cause family |

A concrete example makes it clear. db-train-model answers "ICE 78 left Kassel four minutes late, it will reach Göttingen two minutes late." The multiscale branch answers "S8 towards München Ost departs München Ost about 4 minutes late on average this week."

Both read the same raw archive, but they build different examples from it. That is why the absolute errors are not comparable, and why the route branch cannot simply be swapped in for the trip model in the app. The app's contract asks the first question, not the second.
